analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurers to cover lung cancer screening for everyone 40 and older with no copay.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in June 2020 and died there when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021, without a hearing, vote, or cosponsor from the other chamber.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the preventive-care coverage rules so that private health insurance plans and employer health plans must pay for lung cancer screening for anyone 40 or older, with no deductibles, copays, or other out-of-pocket charges, regardless of whether the person has ever smoked. Today, federal rules require insurers to cover low-dose CT lung screening for free only starting at age 55, and only for people with a significant smoking history. The bill's sponsors point out that lung cancer is the deadliest cancer, that it usually shows no symptoms until late stages, and that catching it early dramatically raises survival rates.
analysis.who_benefits: People 40 and older who are worried about lung cancer but do not meet the current narrow screening criteria—especially never-smokers or light smokers, who are disproportionately women and who currently get no guaranteed free screening—would gain access to screening without paying out of pocket. People facing out-of-pocket costs for a scan today would save hundreds of dollars per screening.

how_it_helps.text: Requires private health plans and insurers to cover lung cancer screenings for individuals 40 and older without any cost sharing, regardless of smoking history.
Removes the current federal coverage standard that begins free lung screening at age 55 and only for people with a heavy smoking history, which excludes never-smokers and light smokers.

The bill's findings state that lung cancer is the top cancer killer and has a 19% overall five-year survival rate because it is hard to detect early, and that early screening could dramatically raise survival.
For all stages of lung cancer, the overall 5-year survival rate is 19 percent, while such rate is 98 percent for prostate cancer and 90 percent for breast cancer (all stages).

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers who sponsor health plans would bear the cost of additional free screenings, and those costs would likely be passed back into premiums for all policyholders. If large numbers of people get screening CT scans, incidental findings can also lead to follow-up testing that adds cost.

drawbacks.text: Screening the entire 40-plus population rather than the current high-risk group would substantially raise screening volume and premiums, since the cost of eliminating copays flows back into insurance prices.

The bill bypasses the established process under which preventive-care coverage requirements are set by independent medical evidence (the US Preventive Services Task Force); the current 55-plus, heavy-smoker criteria reflect that evidence, and a statutory age-40 mandate for everyone regardless of smoking history goes beyond it.
Broad screening can produce false positives and incidental findings that lead to invasive follow-up procedures for people who never had cancer—a recognized trade-off in lung screening policy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Early lung cancer detection genuinely saves lives, and the bill's core idea—free screening for people outside the current narrow criteria—has since gained momentum in actual practice: the US Preventive Services Task Force lowered its recommended starting age to 50 and expanded eligibility in 2021. But this bill was drafted as a hard statutory mandate for everyone 40 and up, well beyond what the medical evidence supports, which would have driven up premiums and exposed many people to false-positive harms. A more targeted expansion might have achieved most of the benefit at lower cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on June 8, 2020, referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee the same day, and sat there with no hearing or vote until the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, which automatically killed it.

narrative.text: Rep. Brendan Boyle introduced the bill on June 8, 2020, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
The bill attracted five Democratic cosponsors and no Republican cosponsors, and no companion legislation in the Senate is listed on its Congress.gov page.
The action history shows no further activity after the initial referral: no committee hearing, no markup, no floor action, through the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer plan sponsors are better off because the bill died, since they avoided a mandate to provide free lung screening to everyone over 40. The bill's sponsors lost the chance to expand access, though the underlying policy idea was later advanced through the US Preventive Services Task Force's 2021 update, which lowered the recommended screening age to 50 for people with a modest smoking history.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers avoided a new mandate

for.name: Rep. Brendan F. Boyle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to mandate free lung cancer screening coverage starting at age 40 regardless of smoking history.

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee to which the bill was referred, never scheduled it for a hearing or markup; the bill sat in committee until Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All five cosponsors were Democrats and none of the 197 House Republicans signed on; the bill died in committee without reaching a vote, so no roll call ever tested broader support.

industries.note: The bill would force insurers and employer plans to pay for lung screening for everyone over 40 with no copay, expanding benefits at their expense. Insurers would likely recoup part of this through higher premiums.

Mandated free screening for all adults over 40 would sharply increase demand for low-dose CT scans and follow-up diagnostics. More scanning means earlier cancer detection for some patients but also more incidental findings and downstream procedures.
